chapters.summary: Ishmael, the narrator, tells the reader to call him Ishmael. He says that when he feels gloomy, he likes to go to sea. He describes crowds of city men staring at the water and says that people are drawn to water. He explains that he always goes to sea as a simple sailor, not as a passenger or officer, because sailors are paid. He says that a strange force, the Fates, guided him toward a whaling voyage. He admits that the great whale drew his curiosity and pulled him toward the trip.
keyEvents: Ishmael says he goes to sea when he feels gloomy
He describes crowds of city men staring at the water
He explains why he always goes to sea as a sailor
He says the Fates guided him toward a whaling voyage
He admits the great whale drew his curiosity
chapters.setting: New York City and the sea
contentNotes: Mentions drowning in the story of Narcissus
Mentions suicidal feelings in a joking way, such as stepping into the street

chapters.summary: Ishmael arrives in New Bedford on a cold Saturday night in December. He wants to sail from Nantucket, but the packet there has already left, so he must wait until Monday. With little money, he walks through dark, cold streets looking for cheap lodging. He passes The Crossed Harpoons and the Sword-Fish Inn, then stumbles into a negro church by mistake. At last he finds The Spouter Inn, run by Peter Coffin, and decides it is the place for cheap lodging. Along the way he reflects on the cold wind Euroclydon and on the rich and the poor.
keyEvents: Ishmael arrives in New Bedford on a cold Saturday night in December
He learns the Nantucket packet has sailed and must wait until Monday
He walks the cold streets looking for cheap lodging
He mistakenly enters a negro church at The Trap
He finds The Spouter Inn, run by Peter Coffin, and decides to stay
chapters.setting: New Bedford streets and The Spouter Inn
contentNotes: Describes a freezing night and a poor man sleeping outside in the cold
Brief religious imagery of damnation and wailing in the church scene

chapters.summary: The narrator enters the Spouter-Inn on a cold night and sees a strange painting and a wall of weapons. The landlord says the room is full, and the narrator must share a bed with a harpooneer. The narrator sees a crowd of seamen come in and notices a quiet Southerner named Bulkington leave. The landlord explains that the harpooneer has been out selling heads. Late at night the narrator finds the harpooneer, Queequeg, who has tattoos and a wooden idol. Queequeg has a tomahawk and frightens the narrator. The landlord calms things down, and the narrator agrees to share the bed. The narrator falls asleep easily in the end.
keyEvents: Narrator sees a strange painting and a wall of weapons in the inn
Landlord says the only bed must be shared with a harpooneer
Seamen from the Grampus arrive and Bulkington leaves
Narrator learns the harpooneer has been selling heads
Queequeg enters the room, makes a fire offering, and threatens the narrator with a tomahawk
chapters.setting: Spouter-Inn, New Bedford
contentNotes: Drinking and drunkenness among sailors
Threatening behavior with a tomahawk
Talk of cannibalism and selling human heads
Mild racial stereotyping and slurs in dialogue

chapters.summary: Narrator wakes at daylight to find Queequeg's tattooed arm wrapped around him in a loving way. He recalls a childhood memory of being sent to bed in daylight and feeling a strange hand in his. Queequeg sleeps on, and the narrator wakes him with great effort. Queequeg gets up, gives the narrator privacy to dress, and then dresses himself, first putting on his hat and boots. He washes only his chest, arms, and hands, then shaves his face with his harpoon. He leaves the room carrying the harpoon.
keyEvents: Narrator wakes to find Queequeg's arm hugging him
Narrator recalls a childhood memory of being sent to bed in daylight
Narrator struggles to wake Queequeg, who finally sits up
Queequeg dresses, putting on his hat and boots first
Queequeg shaves his face with his harpoon
chapters.setting: A bedroom in a strange house
contentNotes: Queequeg is a South Sea islander and is called a cannibal and savage in the text, reflecting outdated 19th-century attitudes

chapters.summary: The narrator goes down to the bar-room and jokes pleasantly with the grinning landlord. The room fills with whalemen, each tanned to show how long he has been ashore. At breakfast the men sit silent and embarrassed, but Queequeg is cool as an icicle. He reaches across the table with his harpoon and pulls the beefsteaks toward him, eating them rare. Afterward he smokes his tomahawk-pipe in the public room, still wearing his hat. The narrator then goes out for a stroll.
keyEvents: Narrator jokes with the landlord in the bar-room
Whalemen gather in the bar-room for breakfast
Men sit silent and embarrassed at the table
Queequeg uses his harpoon to grab beefsteaks
Queequeg smokes his pipe while the narrator goes out for a stroll
chapters.setting: Inn bar-room and breakfast room
contentNotes: Pipe smoking
Harpoon used carelessly at the breakfast table

chapters.summary: Ishmael walks through the streets of New Bedford and finds that the town is full of strange sights. He sees foreign sailors and cannibals standing on street corners, and he notices green country men from Vermont and New Hampshire who have just come to join the whale fishery. He describes these newcomers as comical, with their odd clothes and eager ideas. He also praises the town's rich houses, which he says were paid for by the whale oil trade. He ends by admiring the town's trees, flowers, and women.
keyEvents: Ishmael takes his first daylight walk through New Bedford streets
He notices foreign sailors and cannibals at street corners
He observes green country recruits arriving for the whale fishery
He describes the wealthy houses built with whale oil money
chapters.setting: The streets of New Bedford

chapters.summary: Ishmael went to the Whaleman's Chapel in New Bedford on a cold, stormy Sunday. Sailors, wives, and widows sat apart in silence. Marble tablets on the walls honored men lost at sea, including John Talbot, lost overboard, and Captain Ezekiel Hardy, killed by a whale. Queequeg, who could not read, was the only one who noticed Ishmael enter. Ishmael thought about the mystery of death. Then he grew cheerful again and said his body was not his true self, so a whaling death did not frighten him.
keyEvents: Ishmael enters the chapel during a sleet storm
Reads memorial tablets for sailors lost at sea
Queequeg notices Ishmael's entrance
Reflects on death and the mysteries of the dead
Grows cheerful and cheers for Nantucket and the voyage
chapters.setting: Whaleman's Chapel, New Bedford
contentNotes: Several sailors die at sea, including a boy lost overboard
A captain is killed by a whale
A crew is towed out of sight by a whale
Discussion of death and widows' grief

chapters.summary: Ishmael enters a chapel in the snowy weather and sees Father Mapple, the chaplain, a former sailor and harpooneer. The congregation greets him warmly. He removes his wet hat and coat, then approaches the tall pulpit. The pulpit has no stairs, only a side ladder with red rope ropes, like a ship's ladder. Mapple climbs it sailor-style, then pulls the ladder up after him, shutting himself inside. Ishmael thinks this shows spiritual withdrawal. The wall behind the pulpit holds a painting of a ship in a storm, with an angel's face shining in the sunlight. The pulpit itself is shaped like a ship's bow, and Ishmael says the pulpit leads the world, like a ship's prow.
keyEvents: Father Mapple enters the chapel in wet clothes
Mapple climbs the pulpit's side ladder like a sailor
Mapple pulls the ladder up and seals himself in the pulpit
Ishmael describes the painting of a storm-tossed ship and angel
Ishmael describes the pulpit as shaped like a ship's bow
chapters.setting: A chapel in New Bedford during a winter storm

chapters.summary: Father Mapple, a preacher, leads the congregation in a prayer and a hymn about Jonah and the whale. He then reads from the book of Jonah and preaches a sermon. He describes how Jonah fled from God by boarding a ship bound for Tarshish, paying his fare, and falling asleep in his cabin. A great storm hit the ship, and the sailors cast lots, which chose Jonah. They threw him overboard, and a whale swallowed him. Mapple says Jonah's repentance is a model for sinners. He tells the people that a preacher must speak hard truths. He ends by describing the joy of those who serve God, then kneels alone after the people leave.
keyEvents: Father Mapple leads a prayer and a hymn
Mapple preaches on Jonah fleeing to Tarshish
Jonah pays his fare and sleeps in the ship's cabin
A storm hits and the lot falls on Jonah
Jonah is thrown into the sea and swallowed by a whale
chapters.setting: A whaling chapel
contentNotes: Jonah is thrown into the sea and swallowed by a whale
Storm danger at sea
Mention of a drunken man, murder, and other crimes in a sailor's joke

chapters.summary: Ishmael returns to the Spouter-Inn from the Chapel and finds Queequeg alone by the fire, counting the pages of a big book and whistling in surprise at every fifty. Ishmael watches him and feels drawn to him despite his strange looks. They share a smoke from Queequeg's pipe, and Queequeg says they are now married, meaning bosom friends. He gives Ishmael half of his silver. Before bed, Queequeg prays to his idol, and Ishmael joins him in a small act of worship, reasoning that doing good to a fellow man is true worship. The two then lie in bed and talk.
keyEvents: Ishmael finds Queequeg alone at the inn counting pages
Ishmael admires Queequeg's face and bearing
The two share a smoke and become friends
Queequeg gives Ishmael half his money
Ishmael joins Queequeg's idol worship before bed
chapters.setting: The Spouter-Inn, a room by the fire
contentNotes: Queequeg is described as a 'savage' and 'Pagan' in period language that some readers may find offensive
Ishmael takes part in pagan idol worship, which the text presents as a religious question
Use of tobacco (smoking)

chapters.summary: Ishmael and Queequeg lie in bed at midnight, chatting and napping. They sit up together under the blankets, since the room has no fire. Ishmael reflects on how warmth is felt by contrast with cold, and on why he likes keeping his eyes shut in bed. When he opens them, the dark room feels unpleasant. Queequeg suggests lighting a lamp so he can smoke his pipe, and Ishmael now enjoys sharing it. Queequeg then begins to tell the story of his native island.
keyEvents: Ishmael and Queequeg lie in bed talking and napping
They sit up in bed to stay warm, with no fire in the room
Ishmael opens his eyes and feels the cold, dark room
Queequeg suggests a light and they pass his pipe as the lamp is lit
Queequeg begins to tell the story of his native island
chapters.setting: bedroom at midnight in an inn
contentNotes: Smoking a pipe in bed, with a lit lamp nearby

chapters.summary: Ishmael tells how Queequeg, a prince from the island of Rokovoko, wanted to see Christian lands. A Sag Harbor ship refused to take him, so he hid near a strait and grabbed the deck as it sailed past. The captain let him stay, and the crew made him a whaler. After seeing how sailors behaved in Sag Harbor and Nantucket, Queequeg felt that the world was wicked and said he would die a pagan. He planned to go to sea again. Ishmael said he would sail from Nantucket, and Queequeg agreed to go with him as a harpooneer. That night they smoked and fell asleep.
keyEvents: Queequeg tries to get a ship to take him to Christian lands
He hides in the mangroves and jumps onto the passing ship
The captain lets him stay and he becomes a whaler
He decides Christians are wicked and plans to die a pagan
Queequeg agrees to sail with Ishmael from Nantucket
chapters.setting: Ishmael's lodging, where the two men talk and smoke
contentNotes: Mentions cannibalism as a past practice of Queequeg's people
Describes sailors' bad behavior in port, including spending wages

chapters.summary: On Monday morning Ishmael settles the bill at the inn, using Queequeg's money, and the two friends wheel their belongings down to the Moss, a small schooner at the wharf. Queequeg tells two stories about wheelbarrows and a ship captain at a wedding feast in his homeland. As the schooner sails down the Acushnet river, a young passenger mocks Queequeg, who lifts him into the air and sets him down. The Captain threatens Queequeg, but then the boom breaks loose and nearly sweeps the deck. Queequeg ropes the boom and dives in to rescue the young man, who is pulled from the water alive. The Captain apologizes, and Ishmael becomes close to Queequeg from that day on.
keyEvents: Ishmael settles the inn bill with Queequeg's money
The two friends wheel their belongings to the schooner Moss
Queequeg tells stories about a wheelbarrow and a captain at a wedding feast
A young passenger mocks Queequeg and is thrown into the air
The loose boom threatens the deck and Queequeg ropes it
chapters.setting: New Bedford, then the Acushnet river aboard the schooner Moss
contentNotes: A young passenger is nearly drowned and is revived
Queequeg throws a passenger into the air, causing injury risk
Racial stereotyping and slurs in dialogue about Queequeg
Broken speech of Queequeg reflects period racial caricature

chapters.summary: The ship makes a fine run and safely arrives at Nantucket. The narrator describes the island as a lonely sandy place, with jokes about its poor soil and its people. He then tells an old legend about how the island was first settled. The chapter goes on to praise the Nantucket people as sailors who rule the sea and spend most of their lives on it.
keyEvents: Ship arrives safely at Nantucket after a fine run
Narrator describes the island as a sandy, lonely place
Legend of the eagle and the infant Indian is told
Nantucketers turn from the beach to whaling and sea voyages
Narrator says the Nantucketer rules the sea and lives on it
chapters.setting: Nantucket island, at sea
contentNotes: An infant's death is implied in the legend of the eagle

chapters.summary: Ishmael and Queequeg arrive late at night at the Try Pots, an inn run by Mrs. Hussey in Nantucket. Its sign hangs from an old mast that looks like a gallows. Mrs. Hussey asks whether they want clam or cod, and the chowder is fishy and tasty. Ishmael tests her by asking for cod, and a cod chowder comes out. Mrs. Hussey takes Queequeg's harpoon because a former boarder, Stiggs, was found dead in his room with a harpoon in his side. She keeps the harpoon overnight, and the men order clam or cod for breakfast.
keyEvents: Ishmael and Queequeg arrive late at the Try Pots
Ishmael sees the gallows-like sign and feels uneasy
Mrs. Hussey offers clam or cod for supper
Ishmael asks for cod and gets a cod chowder
Mrs. Hussey takes Queequeg's harpoon
chapters.setting: The Try Pots inn, Nantucket
contentNotes: A former boarder, Stiggs, was found dead with a harpoon in his side (mentioned, not shown)

chapters.summary: Ishmael goes to find a ship with Queequeg, who says his god Yojo wants Ishmael to choose the ship alone. Ishmael finds the Pequod, an old, strange whaling ship, and meets Captain Peleg in a wigwam on deck. Peleg questions him sharply and agrees to sign him on. In the cabin, Captain Bildad, Peleg's partner, sets Ishmael's share of the profits, the lay, at the 300th. They argue loudly, then calm down. Ishmael says Queequeg wants to ship too. Peleg tells him about Captain Ahab, who lost a leg to a whale, and warns him not to mock Ahab's name. Ishmael leaves uneasy about Ahab.
keyEvents: Queequeg says Yojo wants Ishmael to choose the ship alone
Ishmael finds the Pequod and admires her old look
Peleg questions Ishmael and agrees to ship him
Bildad and Peleg argue over Ishmael's lay
Peleg warns Ishmael about Captain Ahab
chapters.setting: Nantucket harbor, the Pequod and her cabin
contentNotes: Heated argument between Peleg and Bildad, with threats of violence
Peleg mentions Ahab's lost leg from a whale attack
Mild religious and cultural language about Quakers and Ramadan

chapters.summary: Ishmael goes to Queequeg's room in the evening and finds the door locked. Queequeg does not answer. Ishmael grows alarmed and runs for help, and the landlady Mrs. Hussey and the chamber-maid join him. When they break the door open, Queequeg is sitting on his hams, holding Yojo on his head, and will not speak or move. Ishmael leaves him there overnight, covers him with his bearskin jacket, and sleeps poorly. At dawn Queequeg stands up and says his Ramadan is over. Ishmael lectures him about religion, but Queequeg seems unmoved. They then eat a large breakfast and head out to board the Pequod.
keyEvents: Ishmael knocks on Queequeg's locked door and gets no answer
Ishmael and the chamber-maid alarm Mrs. Hussey
Door is forced open and Queequeg is found sitting motionless
Ishmael covers Queequeg with his jacket and goes to bed
At dawn Queequeg says his Ramadan is over
chapters.setting: Inn where Ishmael and Queequeg lodge, then the streets toward the Pequod
contentNotes: Ishmael fears Queequeg has had a stroke or killed himself, and the landlady mentions suicide
Queequeg sits motionless for many hours without food
Mention of cannibalism: a sailor's account of a island custom of eating slain enemies after battle

chapters.summary: As the narrator walked toward the ship with Queequeg, Captain Peleg refused to let a cannibal aboard without papers. Captain Bildad questioned Queequeg about his church. The narrator claimed Queequeg was a member of the First Congregational Church. To prove his skill, Queequeg threw his harpoon across the deck and struck a spot of tar on the water. Peleg enrolled him in the crew. Queequeg signed with a tattooed mark. Bildad gave him a tract and warned him about hell. Then Peleg argued that pious harpooneers make poor whalers.
keyEvents: Peleg refuses to let Queequeg board without papers
Bildad questions Queequeg about his church
Queequeg hits a tar spot with his harpoon
Queequeg signs the ship's papers with his tattoo mark
Bildad gives Queequeg a tract and warns him about hell
chapters.setting: Nantucket wharf and the ship's deck and cabin
contentNotes: Characters use slurs such as cannibal, savage, and Philistine for Queequeg
Bildad warns of hell and the fiery pit
Peleg mentions a former sailor who went to Davy Jones (a death reference)

chapters.summary: Ishmael and Queequeg leave the Pequod and walk along the waterfront. A ragged stranger with a scarred face stops them and asks whether they have signed on. He talks strangely about Captain Ahab, mentioning the lost leg, a fight long ago, and a silver calabash, but he will not explain. He gives his name as Elijah. Ishmael decides he is a humbug, but when Ishmael turns a corner he sees Elijah following them. Ishmael tests this by crossing the street, and Elijah walks past without looking at them. Ishmael again decides Elijah is a humbug.
keyEvents: Elijah stops Ishmael and Queequeg and asks if they have shipped on the Pequod
Elijah hints at dark secrets about Captain Ahab and gives his name
Ishmael sees Elijah following them
Ishmael crosses the street to test him, and Elijah walks past
Ishmael again decides Elijah is a humbug
chapters.setting: Waterfront streets near the Pequod, Nantucket
contentNotes: Mentions a sailor's lost leg and a past fight that nearly killed Ahab
Elijah's talk is strange and unsettling, with hints of doom

chapters.summary: Over a day or two, the crew of the Pequod made many last preparations. New sails, rope, and supplies came aboard, and the men worked late into the night. Aunt Charity, Captain Bildad's sister, brought many useful things to the ship. Captain Peleg shouted orders from his wigwam, and Bildad checked items off his list. Queequeg and the narrator visited often and asked about Captain Ahab. They were told he was getting better and would come aboard soon. At last, they learned the ship would sail the next day, so they set out very early.
keyEvents: Pequod receives sails, rigging, and stores before sailing
Aunt Charity brings supplies to the ship
Queequeg and the narrator visit and ask about Ahab, who is said to be recovering
News comes that the ship will sail next day, and the two set out early
chapters.setting: The Pequod and the Island, where the ship is being readied

chapters.summary: At dawn, the narrator and Queequeg walked toward the Pequod. On the wharf, a strange man named Elijah stopped them with odd questions and warnings, then walked away. On board, the ship was quiet, and they found an old rigger asleep in the forecastle. Queequeg sat on the sleeper and smoked his tomahawk pipe, which woke the man. The rigger said Captain Ahab had come aboard the night before and that the ship would sail that day. Soon the crew arrived, but Ahab stayed hidden in his cabin.
keyEvents: Elijah stops the narrator and Queequeg on the wharf and asks strange questions
They board the Pequod and find an old rigger asleep in the forecastle
Queequeg sits on the sleeper and smokes his tomahawk pipe
The rigger wakes and says the ship sails today and Ahab came aboard last night
The crew and shore people arrive at sunrise while Ahab stays in his cabin
chapters.setting: New Bedford wharf and the forecastle of the Pequod at dawn
contentNotes: Elijah makes cryptic, unsettling remarks
Queequeg jokingly waves a tomahawk over a sleeping man and says it would be easy to kill him
Pipe smoking in a closed space
Queequeg describes a custom of fattening people to use as furniture

chapters.summary: On Christmas, after the crew finished their last jobs, the Pequod left port. Captain Peleg and Captain Bildad gave the orders, and Captain Ahab stayed below in the cabin, saying he was not yet fully recovered. Peleg shouted and kicked the sailors at the windlass while Bildad sang hymns. Once the anchor was up and the ship was out at sea, Bildad sang a hymn as pilot. The two captains then left the ship in a boat, Bildad sad to go. The crew gave three cheers as the ship sailed into the Atlantic.
keyEvents: Pequod hauled out from the wharf and prepared to sail
Peleg orders crew to raise the anchor while Bildad sings
Ship sets sail on a cold Christmas night
Bildad sings a hymn while steering as pilot
Peleg and Bildad leave the ship by boat
chapters.setting: The Pequod, leaving port and sailing into the Atlantic
contentNotes: Peleg uses harsh language and swearing
Peleg kicks a sailor

chapters.summary: On a freezing winter night, the Pequod sailed out to sea. The narrator saw Bulkington standing at her helm. Bulkington had just come home from a four-year voyage, yet he set out again at once. The narrator watched him with awe and fear. He compared Bulkington to a storm-tossed ship that must keep away from the shore, even though the harbor offered safety. The narrator said that deep thinking is the soul's effort to stay free on the open sea. He urged Bulkington to bear up and rise from the spray.
keyEvents: Pequod sails out on a winter night
Narrator sees Bulkington at the helm
Narrator compares Bulkington to a ship avoiding the lee shore
Narrator urges Bulkington to endure
chapters.setting: Aboard the Pequod at sea, leaving port in winter

chapters.summary: The narrator defended whaling against landsmen who looked down on it. He said whalemen were butchers, but so were famous military commanders. He argued that whaling had opened remote lands, helped free Peru, Chili, and Bolivia, and shaped Australia and Polynesia. He pointed to royal honors, famous writers, and Benjamin Franklin's family as proof of its dignity. He ended by saying the whale-ship had been his true college.
keyEvents: Narrator defends whaling against landsmen's low opinion
Argues whaling is as bloody as military conquest but more useful
Lists whaling's influence on exploration, trade, and freedom in South America
Cites royal honors, famous writers, and Franklin's family as signs of whaling's dignity
Declares the whale-ship was his true education
chapters.setting: No specific setting; general discussion of whaling
contentNotes: Discusses the killing and butchering of whales in general terms
Brief references to battlefield carnage and soldiers' deaths

chapters.summary: The narrator defends the dignity of whaling by arguing that a king's coronation oil must be sperm oil. He jokes about the oiling of a king's head and the seasoning of rulers with salt. He calls on loyal Britons to think of whalemen as suppliers of coronation oil. Nothing happens in the chapter except this argument.
keyEvents: Narrator defends whaling's dignity with a suspicion about royal oil
Narrator jokes about the salt and oiling used at coronations
Narrator concludes that sperm oil must be the coronation oil
chapters.setting: Unspecified; the narrator's essay addresses readers

chapters.summary: The narrator described Starbuck, the chief mate of the Pequod. Starbuck was a Nantucket man of Quaker descent, thin, hard, and steady. He had a deep reverence and leaned toward superstition. Memories of his wife and child softened his rough nature. Starbuck said he wanted no man in his boat who was not afraid of a whale. Stubb, the second mate, called Starbuck careful. The narrator then praised the dignity of common workers and asked God to support his writing about them.
keyEvents: Starbuck is introduced as chief mate
Starbuck says he wants no man in his boat who is not afraid of a whale
Stubb calls Starbuck careful
Narrator praises the dignity of common workers
chapters.setting: aboard the Pequod
contentNotes: Men killed by whales are mentioned
Starbuck's father and brother are lost at sea

chapters.summary: The narrator introduced the Pequod's three mates: Stubb, Flask, and Starbuck. Stubb, a Cape Cod man, was easygoing and seemed unafraid, and he smoked his pipe constantly. Flask, a short, ruddy man from Tisbury, was pugnacious and eager to kill whales. Each mate had a harpooneer as his squire, including Queequeg, Tashtego, and Daggoo. The narrator then described the crew, many of whom were not American-born, and called such men Isolatoes. The chapter ends by recalling Pip, who went before.
keyEvents: Stubb's easygoing nature and pipe-smoking described
Flask's hostility toward whales described
Harpooneers named as squires to the mates
Crew's mixed origins described
Pip's fate recalled
chapters.setting: Aboard the Pequod
contentNotes: References to death, including Pip's implied death
Mention of cholera and disease

chapters.summary: After the Pequod leaves Nantucket, the narrator watches for Captain Ahab, who stays hidden in his cabin while the mates run the ship. When Ahab finally comes on deck, the narrator sees his scarred face and bone leg. Ahab stands fixed in an auger hole, staring ahead with a look of deep woe. Each day he appears more often as the weather warms. Slowly, the mild spring air seems to soften his gloomy mood, and he almost smiles.
keyEvents: Ahab stays hidden in his cabin after the ship leaves Nantucket
Ahab first appears on the quarter-deck on a gray morning
The narrator describes Ahab's white scar and ivory leg
Ahab stands fixed in an auger hole, staring out to sea
Ahab appears more often as the weather warms and nearly smiles
chapters.setting: Aboard the Pequod, at sea after leaving Nantucket
contentNotes: Ahab's leg is described as made from sperm whale jawbone
Mentions of a superstitious claim that Ahab was branded in a sea strife

chapters.summary: Days pass as the Pequod sails through warm, clear weather near the Tropic. Ahab, who rarely sleeps, comes up at night and paces the deck. His heavy ivory heel is loud, so Stubb suggests muffling it. Ahab angrily calls Stubb a dog and orders him below. Stubb is shaken and does not know what to make of the old captain. He goes back to his hammock and decides to sleep on it, thinking Ahab must be troubled by something.
keyEvents: Pequod sails through calm, warm weather
Ahab paces the deck at night
Stubb suggests muffling Ahab's ivory heel
Ahab angrily calls Stubb a dog and orders him below
Stubb goes to his hammock, puzzled and shaken
chapters.setting: Deck and cabin of the Pequod at night
contentNotes: Ahab angrily insults Stubb and threatens to clear the world of him
Mild drinking-free; mentions of sharks in passing

chapters.summary: Ahab sits on his ivory stool on the weather side of the deck and smokes his pipe. He thinks about kings and royalty as he looks at himself. He starts to feel that smoking no longer brings him comfort. He says his pipe is meant for calm old men, not for a man with grey hair like his. He throws the lit pipe into the sea and paces the deck with his hat pulled low.
keyEvents: Ahab sends for his ivory stool and pipe
Ahab smokes on the weather side of the deck
Ahab decides smoking no longer soothes him
Ahab throws his lit pipe into the sea
Ahab paces the planks with his hat slouched
chapters.setting: Deck of the Pequod

chapters.summary: Stubb tells Flask about a strange dream he had. In the dream he kicked at Ahab's pyramid, and a humpbacked merman told him that being kicked by Ahab was an honor and that he should never kick back. Stubb says the dream made him wise. Then a voice from the masthead calls out that whales are nearby, and a white one should be hunted. Stubb says something special is in the wind, and Ahab comes near.
keyEvents: Stubb tells Flask about his dream of kicking Ahab's pyramid
Merman in the dream calls Stubb wise and says to accept Ahab's kicks as honors
Masthead cry announces whales nearby, including a white one
Stubb warns Flask that Ahab has something bloody on his mind
Ahab approaches
chapters.setting: Aboard the Pequod, on deck
contentNotes: Ahab's ivory leg kick is mentioned as an insult
Dream imagery of a kicked leg and a merman with marlinspikes in his stern

chapters.summary: The narrator offers a rough system for sorting whales. He begins by noting how little real knowledge exists, and lists many earlier writers on whales. He argues that the whale is a fish, using his own definition: a spouting fish with a horizontal tail. He then divides whales into three groups by size: Folio, Octavo, and Duodecimo. Each group is described, with notes on the Sperm Whale, Right Whale, Grampus, Narwhale, Huzza Porpoise, and others. He admits his system is unfinished and says he is only sketching a draft.
keyEvents: Narrator begins describing the study of whales
Narrator defines a whale as a spouting fish with a horizontal tail
Narrator divides whales into Folio, Octavo, and Duodecimo groups
Narrator describes the Sperm Whale and other Folio whales
Narrator describes Octavo and Duodecimo whales
chapters.setting: Narrator's writing about whales, aboard or near the Pequod
contentNotes: Killer whales are described as attacking and worrying larger whales to death
Porpoise and whale oil are described as valued commodities

chapters.summary: The narrator explained a custom on whaling ships. Long ago in the old Dutch whale fishery, the Specksnyder, or chief harpooneer, shared command of the ship and ruled the whale hunt. Later he became a lower officer, but he still ate and slept apart from the crew. The narrator noted that officers kept strict rules of rank at sea. He then turned to Captain Ahab, who used these forms to hide his private wishes and gain power over his men. He called Ahab a grand but rough old whale-hunter.
keyEvents: Narrator explains the history of the Specksnyder, or chief harpooneer
Narrator describes how harpooneers live apart from the crew
Narrator explains the strict rules of rank on ships
Narrator reflects on how Captain Ahab used those forms for power
chapters.setting: Whaling ships in general, no single scene

chapters.summary: At noon, Dough-Boy, the steward, called the officers to dinner. Ahab went down first, then Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask. Flask danced a hornpipe before he went below. At Ahab's table, the officers stayed quiet and nervous, and Flask was always hungry. Later the harpooneers, Queequeg, Tashtego, and Daggoo, ate loudly in the cabin and frightened poor Dough-Boy. The chapter ends with a reflection on Ahab, who lived alone in his gloom like a bear in winter.
keyEvents: Dough-Boy announces dinner to Ahab
Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask go down to dinner in turn
Flask dances a hornpipe on the quarter-deck
Officers sit silently at Ahab's table
Harpooneers eat loudly and frighten Dough-Boy
chapters.setting: The Pequod's deck and cabin
contentNotes: Tashtego threatens to scalp Dough-Boy as a joke; Daggoo stuffs Dough-Boy's head into a trencher
Cannibalism is joked about (Queequeg's past, Dough-Boy as a waiter to cannibals)
A rat makes noise in the hold

chapters.summary: The narrator gets his first turn at the mast-head, the high lookout post on a whaling ship. He explains that the custom is very old and tells of ancient and modern figures who stood high places. He describes the mast-head as a lonely, sleepy place with little comfort. He praises Captain Sleet's crow's-nest on the Glacier, a shelter used by Greenland whalers. He admits he did not keep careful watch, since his mind wandered. He warns ship-owners against dreamy young men who gaze at the sea and forget to look for whales.
keyEvents: Narrator's first mast-head turn comes around
Narrator lists ancient and modern figures who stood high places
Narrator describes the discomfort of the southern whaler's mast-head
Narrator praises Captain Sleet's crow's-nest
Narrator admits he kept poor watch and warns against dreamy young men
chapters.setting: Whaling ship at sea, in the tropics
contentNotes: Mentions a man who dies at his post (Saint Stylites, historical)
Ends with a warning of a drowning fall from the mast-head and a figure who loses his identity

chapters.summary: One morning after breakfast, Ahab walks the deck and then calls the whole crew aft. He asks what they do when they see a whale, and the men shout eager answers. He nails a gold ounce to the mainmast as a reward for whoever first spots the white whale with a wrinkled brow, crooked jaw, and three holes in its starboard fluke. Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg say they know the whale as Moby Dick. Ahab admits Moby Dick took his leg and swears to chase it anywhere. Starbuck objects that vengeance on a dumb animal is madness, but Ahab pulls him in. Ahab then has the harpooneers and mates drink grog and swear an oath to hunt Moby Dick to his death.
keyEvents: Ahab calls the entire crew aft
Ahab asks the crew what they do when they see a whale
Ahab nails a gold ounce to the mainmast as a reward
Tashtego, Daggoo, and Queequeg identify the whale as Moby Dick

chapters.setting: The quarter-deck of the Pequod
contentNotes: Ahab's obsessive vengeance against the whale, which took his leg
Heavy drinking of grog by the crew
A ritual oath of death to Moby Dick, with harpoon-socket goblets of liquor

chapters.summary: Ahab sat alone in the cabin and watched the sun set. He felt weighed down by pain and anger, like a heavy iron crown. He said sunset no longer brought him joy, and that he was cursed even amid beauty. He vowed that he would not be turned aside. He said he would take revenge on the one that cost him his leg. He spoke of his purpose as an iron track that nothing could block.
keyEvents: Ahab sits alone in the cabin watching the sunset
He describes his heavy iron crown and his inner pain
He says beauty brings him only anguish
He vows to dismember his dismemberer
He declares his purpose cannot be swerved
chapters.setting: ship's cabin by the stern windows
contentNotes: Ahab speaks of his lost leg and seeks revenge
Ahab describes himself as mad and damned, with despair

chapters.summary: Starbuck leaned against the mainmast and spoke alone. He said Ahab, the mad captain, had overpowered his reason and tied him to a hunt for the white whale. He felt trapped, like a man bound by a cable he had no knife to cut. Revelry burst from the forecastle while Ahab brooded in his cabin. Starbuck felt the horror of life within him, but he called on blessed influences to hold and help him fight his grim fears.
keyEvents: Starbuck leans against the mainmast and speaks alone
He complains that Ahab has overpowered his reason
Revelry bursts from the forecastle
He calls on blessed influences to help him fight his fears
chapters.setting: Ship's deck by the mainmast
contentNotes: Dark mood of despair and dread
References to a 'heathen crew' and 'infernal orgies'

chapters.summary: Stubb sat alone in the fore-top, mending a brace. He laughed loudly and sang a drinking song about love and bubbles. He said he felt cheerful and would face whatever came with a laugh. He thought Starbuck looked troubled after some talk, and he believed Starbuck's fate was already settled. Then Starbuck called him, and Stubb answered that he was just finishing his job and was on his way.
keyEvents: Stubb mends a brace alone in the fore-top
He laughs and sings a drinking song
He muses that Starbuck looks troubled
Starbuck calls him and he answers he is coming
chapters.setting: The fore-top of the ship

chapters.summary: At midnight the sailors on the forecastle sang and danced while Pip played a tambourine. The sky darkened and the wind rose. Some men kept dancing, some went below, and some lay down to sleep. The Spanish sailor and the harpooneer Daggoo insulted each other, and a fight almost broke out. Then a squall struck the ship. The mate called the crew to reef the sails, and the men scattered to their work. Pip, hiding under the windlass, prayed for mercy and spoke fearfully of the white whale.
keyEvents: Sailors sing and dance on the forecastle
Sky darkens and wind rises
Spanish sailor and Daggoo insult each other and nearly fight
Squall hits and crew scatters to reef sails
Pip hides and prays, fearing the white whale
chapters.setting: Ship's forecastle at midnight
contentNotes: Racial insults between Daggoo and the Spanish sailor
Near fight with a knife mentioned
Drinking of wine
Swearing and oaths
Dangerous squall at sea

chapters.summary: Ishmael, one of the crew, describes the history of the White Whale, Moby Dick. Few whalemen had fought him, and rumors grew wild, so many hunters feared him. Stories said he was ubiquitous and nearly immortal. His white forehead and hump made him easy to spot, and his tricks made him more terrifying. In one fight, Moby Dick bit off Ahab's leg. Ahab then became mad with hate for the whale. On the voyage home he raved in his hammock and was tied down. Later he hid his rage and sailed again with one aim: revenge on the White Whale. Ishmael ends by saying he too was swept up in the mood and saw only evil in the whale.
keyEvents: Moby Dick's history and rumors spread among whalemen
Moby Dick bites off Ahab's leg during a boat battle
Ahab's madness grows during the homeward voyage
Ahab hides his madness and sails again to hunt the White Whale
chapters.setting: Whaling grounds at sea and the Pequod's crew, with Nantucket recalled
contentNotes: Ahab loses a leg in an attack by the whale
Several whalemen are killed or maimed by the whale in past encounters
Ahab is described as raving and tied into his hammock during delirium

chapters.summary: Ishmael explains the strange horror that the whiteness of the whale caused him. He lists many cultures where white meant purity, honor, or royalty. Yet whiteness also made polar bears, white sharks, and ghosts seem more terrifying. He remembered an albatross on a ship's deck and a captain who hooked one, tagged it, and let it go. He described the White Steed of the Prairies and the ruined city of Lima. He suggested that whiteness stands for the empty, deathlike universe. The Albino whale, he said, was the symbol of all these things.
keyEvents: Narrator sees an albatross on the ship's deck during a gale
Captain catches an albatross with a hook, ties a tally to it, and releases it
Narrator argues that whiteness makes certain creatures and sights more frightening
chapters.setting: At sea, with examples from around the world
contentNotes: A bird is caught on a hook and line
Mention of a historical murder by the White Hoods of Ghent
References to death, ghosts, and corpses

chapters.summary: During the middle watch, under a fair moonlight, sailors pass buckets of water in silence to fill the scuttle-butt. Archy hears a noise under the after-hatches and thinks it sounds like a cough and sleepers turning over. His neighbor Cabaco doubts him and says it is only the biscuits he ate for supper. Archy insists he has sharp ears. He suspects someone hidden in the after-hold has never been seen on deck, and he thinks Captain Ahab knows about it. He recalls Stubb saying something of that sort was in the wind.
keyEvents: Archy hears a noise under the after-hatches during the middle watch
Cabaco brushes off the noise and tells Archy to keep working
Archy insists he has sharp ears
Archy suspects someone unseen is hidden in the after-hold
chapters.setting: Deck of the Pequod at night, middle watch

chapters.summary: After a squall, Ahab goes to his cabin and studies old sea charts spread on his table. He marks courses using old logbooks that record where sperm whales were seen. He believes the whale hunters' knowledge of whale migrations can help him find Moby Dick. He knows Moby Dick has returned to the same waters for several years, called the Season-on-the-Line. The Pequod sailed too early to reach those waters this year, so Ahab must wait a full year. He hunts in other seas during that time. Ahab's obsession keeps him awake and haunted. At night he bursts from his room in horror, and the narrator describes his tormented mind as a separate force within him.
keyEvents: Ahab studies charts in his cabin after the squall
Ahab reasons about whale migrations and Moby Dick's habits
Ahab realizes the Pequod must wait a year for the Season-on-the-Line
Ahab is tormented by dreams and bursts from his room in horror
chapters.setting: Ahab's cabin aboard the Pequod
contentNotes: Obsessive revenge theme
Mention of Ahab's bloody nails in his palms from clenched hands
Disturbing dream and psychological torment imagery

chapters.summary: Ishmael argues that sperm whales are powerful and clever enough to attack and sink ships. He tells of a whale that struck and destroyed a few whale hunters' ships. He describes a whale that returned to find a harpooned hunter three years later and killed him. He also tells of a sea monster in the Propontis that destroyed ships for more than fifty years. He gives these stories to show that the story of Moby Dick is believable.
keyEvents: Ishmael describes a whale that escaped and was killed three years later by the same harpooner
Ishmael names famous whales such as Timor Tom and Don Miguel
The Essex is rammed and sunk by a sperm whale in 1820
Commodore J—— is struck by a whale and forced to repair his ship
Ishmael cites Langsdorff and Lionel Wafer's accounts of whale strikes
chapters.setting: Essay on whaling history, with stories from the Pacific, the Azores, and Constantinople
contentNotes: Ships are sunk and sailors die at sea
Whale attacks and deaths during whaling are described

chapters.summary: Ahab thought about why he must keep the Pequod's ordinary whaling work going while he hunts Moby Dick. He feared Starbuck secretly opposed the quest and might rebel. He believed the crew needed daily tasks and some hope of money to stay loyal. Ahab also worried that others might call his command unfair, since he had already revealed his true purpose. So he chose to act like an eager whaling captain. His voice was heard calling the three mast-heads to keep a sharp lookout, even for a porpoise. Soon, their watching was rewarded.
keyEvents: Ahab reasons he must keep ordinary whaling work going
Ahab worries about crew unrest and Starbuck's possible rebellion
Ahab orders the three mast-heads to keep a sharp lookout
The lookout is soon rewarded
chapters.setting: Aboard the Pequod at sea

chapters.summary: On a cloudy afternoon, Ishmael and Queequeg weave a sword-mat on the deck while the crew rests. Ishmael thinks about fate, chance, and free will as he works. Tashtego, high in the cross-trees, shouts that he sees whales blowing off the lee-beam. The crew gets excited and the ship turns toward the whales. Ahab orders the time kept, and the boats are lowered over the side. Just as the boats are ready, Ahab appears with five dark figures who seem to have come out of the air.
keyEvents: Ishmael and Queequeg weave a sword-mat on a still afternoon
Ishmael reflects on fate, chance, and free will
Tashtego spots whales from the cross-trees
Ahab times the whales and the ship turns toward them
Boats are lowered over the sea
chapters.setting: Whaling ship at sea, deck and cross-trees

chapters.summary: Ahab orders the boats lowered from the Pequod, and the strange crew of Fedallah, with their yellow-skinned companions, joins the chase. Starbuck, Stubb, and Flask spread out across the sea while Stubb urges his crew with loud, odd shouts. The boats close in on a school of whales. Queequeg darts his harpoon, but the whale escapes, and a squall strikes. Starbuck lights a lantern and hands it to Queequeg. At dawn the narrator and the crew leap into the sea as the ship comes near. They are picked up and taken safely back on board.
keyEvents: Ahab orders the boats lowered and the strange crew joins them
Ahab and the boats spread out to search for whales
Whales are sighted and the boats give chase
Queequeg's harpoon grazes the whale, which escapes
A squall swamps the boat and the crew is scattered
chapters.setting: the open sea near the Pequod
contentNotes: the crew is nearly drowned in a squall
a whale is harpooned

chapters.summary: After a boat is capsized in a squall near a whale, the narrator feels a strange, carefree mood about the dangers of whaling. He asks Queequeg, Mr. Stubb, and Mr. Flask about the risks. Stubb and Flask answer that such accidents are common and that the boat's steering is blamed on Starbuck, who drove toward the whale in a storm. The narrator decides to make a rough draft of his will. Queequeg is asked to act as his lawyer, executor, and legatee. The narrator feels relieved after finishing the will and accepts the dangers ahead.
keyEvents: Narrator is pulled from the water after the boat capsizes
Narrator asks Stubb and Flask about the risks of whaling
Narrator decides to draft his will
Narrator names Queequeg as lawyer, executor, and legatee
Narrator feels relieved and ready to face danger
chapters.setting: The sea near a whale during a squall, then below deck
contentNotes: A boat capsizes in a storm and crew are thrown into the water
Talk of death and drowning risk

chapters.summary: Stubb and Flask talk about Captain Ahab, who has one leg missing, and his ability to go out in a whale boat. The narrator explains that whaling captains are usually kept out of boat danger. Ahab secretly prepared a boat for himself, shaping its thole-pins, sheathing, and thigh board to fit his ivory leg. Crew members noticed but mostly thought he was preparing for the hunt of Moby Dick. The narrator then describes Fedallah, a strange, mysterious man who seems linked to Ahab and whom no one understands.
keyEvents: Stubb and Flask marvel at Ahab's ability to join the whaling boats
The narrator questions whether a maimed captain should enter a whale boat
Ahab secretly prepares a boat and its crew
The crew notices Ahab's careful work on the boat but thinks little of it
Fedallah is introduced as a mysterious figure linked to Ahab
chapters.setting: Aboard the Pequod, at sea

chapters.summary: The Pequod sailed through several cruising grounds near the Carrol Ground. One moonlit night Fedallah spotted a silvery spout, and the crew hoped for a lowering, but the spout vanished each time they chased it. Some sailors believed it was always Moby Dick, leading them on. Later, rounding the Cape of Good Hope in stormy weather, the crew stood silent in bowlines while Ahab stood gazing to windward. Starbuck saw Ahab asleep in his chair in the cabin, still in his wet coat, and thought him steadfast in his purpose.
keyEvents: Fedallah first sights a silvery spout at night
Crew chases the spout but it disappears again
Sailors believe the spout is always Moby Dick
Storm rounds the Cape of Good Hope
Starbuck sees Ahab asleep in his cabin chair
chapters.setting: The Pequod at sea, near the Carrol Ground and Cape of Good Hope

chapters.summary: The Pequod sailed southeast from the Cape and met a whaler called the Albatross. The other ship was bleached pale and rusty, and its look-outs looked worn from nearly four years at sea. When the stranger asked if they had seen the White Whale, his trumpet fell into the sea. Ahab shouted across that the Pequod was bound round the world. Small fish darted away from the Pequod toward the other ship, and Ahab murmured that they swam away from him. He then ordered the ship kept round the world. The narrator reflects that sailing around the globe only returns a ship to where it started.
keyEvents: Pequod meets the Albatross, a long-absent whaler
Other captain's trumpet falls into the sea
Ahab hails the stranger about the White Whale and his voyage
Small fish flee from the Pequod toward the other ship
Ahab orders the ship kept round the world
chapters.setting: Southeast of the Cape, off the Crozetts

chapters.summary: Ahab does not board the whaler they have hailed, because the wind and sea look stormy and because he only wants news he can use. The narrator explains how whaling ships meet and sociably exchange news, letters, and papers on the open sea. He contrasts whalers with merchant ships, men-of-war, slave ships, and pirates, which keep their distance or treat each other coldly. He explains the word gam and describes how the captain is rowed to a gam standing in the boat, since whale-boats have no seat or tiller for him.
keyEvents: Ahab does not board the hailed whaler
Narrator explains how whaling ships meet and exchange news
Narrator contrasts whalers with other ships
Narrator defines the word gam
Narrator describes the standing captain in the whale-boat
chapters.setting: The open sea near a whaling cruising-ground
contentNotes: Pirates and their hanging mentioned in passing
Slave ships mentioned in passing

chapters.summary: At the Golden Inn in Lima, an old sailor tells Don Pedro and Don Sebastian the story of the Town-Ho. The ship had a leak and sailed for port. Radney, the mate, bullied Steelkilt, a Lakeman, and struck him with a hammer. Steelkilt fought back and led a mutiny. The captain locked the crew below for days. Radney was later killed by Moby Dick when he fell from a boat. Steelkilt's crew then deserted, and Steelkilt escaped to Tahiti. The sailor swears the tale is true.
keyEvents: Town-Ho has a leak and sails for port
Radney hits Steelkilt with a hammer during a dispute over sweeping the deck
Steelkilt leads a mutiny and the crew barricades the forecastle
Captain locks the mutineers below and later hangs three of them in the rigging
Radney is killed by Moby Dick after falling from a boat
chapters.setting: Golden Inn in Lima, and the Town-Ho at sea in the Pacific
contentNotes: Radney's jaw is smashed with a hammer, a violent blow
Mutineers are beaten with a rope and hung in the rigging
A man is killed and eaten by a whale, described in graphic terms
Men are locked in a dark forecastle with little food and water
Some mention of drinking (chicha) at the inn

chapters.summary: Ishmael explains that pictures of the whale are almost always wrong. He starts with ancient sculptures from India, Egypt, and Greece, then mocks paintings by Guido and Hogarth. He criticizes old book prints, a Dutch voyage plate, Captain Colnett's drawing, and Goldsmith's natural history. He also faults Lacepede and Frederick Cuvier, whose sperm whale he calls a squash. Sign-painters' whales are no better. Ishmael argues that dead whales on land cannot show the living shape, and that the skeleton tells little either. He concludes the whale must remain unpainted, and that only a whaling voyage reveals his true look.
keyEvents: Ishmael says pictures of the whale have long been wrong
He criticizes ancient Hindoo and Christian paintings of the whale
He mocks old book prints, a Dutch plate, and Captain Colnett's drawing
He criticizes Lacepede and Frederick Cuvier's whale pictures
He argues the whale's true shape cannot be captured in a portrait
chapters.setting: Not a specific place; a discussion of whale pictures
contentNotes: Mentions whales stoving and sinking whaleboats and sailors, and a sailor being eaten in a sign-painter's picture

chapters.summary: Ishmael compares pictures of whales and whaling scenes. He says Beale's drawings of the Sperm Whale are the best outlines he knows. He praises two large French engravings by Garnery, one of a Sperm Whale attack and one of a Right Whale attack. He says the French capture the real action of whaling better than English and American artists, who mostly draw plain outlines. He also describes two more French engravings by H. Durand, one of a calm anchored ship and one of a ship cutting in a whale.
keyEvents: Ishmael praises Beale's outlines of the Sperm Whale
Ishmael describes Garnery's engraving of a Sperm Whale attack
Ishmael describes Garnery's engraving of a Right Whale attack
Ishmael says the French paint whaling action better than others
Ishmael describes two engravings by H. Durand
chapters.setting: Ishmael's discussion of whaling pictures
contentNotes: Descriptions of whales being attacked and whales dying in engravings

chapters.summary: Ishmael describes many ways people have shown whales in art and objects. He mentions a beggar on Tower-hill who paints a board of a whale attack that cost him his leg. He describes sailors carving whale scenes on teeth and bone with jack-knives, called skrimshander work. He notes wooden whales in forecastles, brass whale knockers, and sheet-iron weathercocks. He tells of rock shapes that look like whales and hills with whale profiles. He ends by saying he has seen whales among the stars and wishes he could ride one into the sky.
keyEvents: A beggar on Tower-hill shows a painted board of a whale attack
Sailors carve whale scenes on teeth and bone with jack-knives
Whales appear as wooden carvings, door knockers, and weathercocks
Rock formations and hill ridges look like whales
Ishmael sees whales and boats among the stars
chapters.setting: Tower-hill in London, sailors' workplaces, and various lands and skies
contentNotes: A man lost his leg in a whale attack (described in a painting)

chapters.summary: The ship sailed north-east from the Crozetts into vast meadows of brit, a tiny yellow substance that Right Whales feed on. The whales swam through it with open jaws, and their movement made a sound like mowers cutting grass. From the mast-heads, the whales looked like lifeless rocks. The narrator reflected that the sea is a dangerous foe to people and even to its own creatures. He compared the sea to the dangers that surround the soul of man.
keyEvents: Ship sails north-east into vast fields of brit
Right Whales swim through brit with open jaws
Whales make a sound like mowers cutting grass
Narrator says whales look like rocks from the mast-heads
Narrator reflects on the sea's cruelty and danger to humans
chapters.setting: Open sea north-east of the Crozetts
contentNotes: General references to shipwrecks, drowning, and sea creatures killing each other
Brief mention of a shark as treacherous

chapters.summary: The Pequod sails slowly north-east toward Java in calm weather. Daggoo sees a white shape rise from the sea and cries out that it is the White Whale. Ahab orders the boats lowered, and the crew pulls toward the spot. Instead of a whale, a huge pulpy squid mass rises and then sinks. Starbuck cries out that he would rather have fought Moby Dick than seen this white ghost. Flask asks what it is, and Ahab answers that it is the great live squid. Ahab turns his boat and sails back to the ship, and the others follow. The narrator then explains what whalemen believe about the squid, compares it to the Kraken, and notes that some naturalists count it among the cuttle-fish.
keyEvents: Daggoo sights a white shape from the main-mast-head
Ahab orders the boats lowered
Crew finds a huge pulpy squid instead of a whale
Starbuck cries out about the white ghost
Ahab turns back to the ship and the others follow
chapters.setting: The open sea, sailing north-east toward Java

chapters.summary: This chapter explains the whale-line used in whaling. The narrator describes the material, first hemp and then Manilla rope, and how the line is coiled in a tub without any tangles. He tells how the line is laid through the whale-boat and attached to the harpoon. He describes how the crew feels seated among the coils, and how danger can strike suddenly. No new plot events happen. The narrator ends by saying that all people live surrounded by dangers they do not notice until death is near.
keyEvents: Narrator describes hemp and Manilla whale-line
Line is coiled carefully in the tub
Line is run through the boat to the harpoon
Narrator reflects on the danger of sitting among the coils
chapters.setting: A whale-boat and the whaling fishery
contentNotes: References to men being pulled from boats and lost at sea
Figurative mention of death and hangman's nooses

chapters.summary: The Pequod's crew sits in a calm, sleepy sea. Ishmael, on the masthead, nearly falls asleep. A huge sperm whale appears close to the ship, and Ahab orders the boats lowered. The men paddle quietly after the whale until it notices them and dives. Stubb, smoking his pipe, races ahead to claim the kill. Tashtego throws the harpoon, and the line burns through Stubb's hands as the whale pulls the boat across the sea. The crew hauls the boat close, and Stubb drives his lance deep into the whale. The whale's heart bursts, and Daggoo announces that it is dead. Stubb stands looking at the dead whale.
keyEvents: Crew drowses in the calm sea
Ishmael and others nearly fall asleep at the masthead
Sperm whale appears close to the ship
Ahab orders the boats lowered and the chase begins
Whale notices the boats and Stubb races ahead
chapters.setting: Indian Ocean, aboard the Pequod and in its whaleboats
contentNotes: A whale is hunted and killed, with blood and a violent death described in detail
Stubb's hands are burned by the running line
Stubb smokes a pipe throughout

chapters.summary: The narrator added a note about an earlier incident in the whale-boat chase. He explained that the harpooneer must row hard and shout, then stand and throw the harpoon while exhausted. Few darts succeeded, and some harpooneers were cursed or hurt. He argued that the headsman should stay in the bows and not row, since exhaustion, not the whale's speed, caused most failures. He concluded that harpooneers should start the dart fresh, not worn out.
keyEvents: Narrator explains the harpooneer's duties during a chase
Harpooneer is too exhausted to throw the harpoon well
Most darts fail and harpooneers are blamed
Narrator says the headsman should stay in the bows
Narrator concludes harpooneers must start fresh, not worn out
chapters.setting: General discussion of whale-boats in the fishery
contentNotes: Some harpooneers burst their blood-vessels from exertion

chapters.summary: This chapter explains the crotch, a notched stick fixed to the starboard gunwale near the bow. It holds the harpoon ready for the harpooneer to grab quickly. Two harpoons, the first and second irons, usually rest in the crotch, and both are tied to the line so that one may hold if the other pulls out. When the whale runs hard after the first iron, the second iron is often thrown overboard, where it dangles and can tangle or cut lines. This act sometimes causes deadly accidents. The narrator says these details will help explain later scenes.
keyEvents: Crotch described as a notched stick on the starboard gunwale
First and second irons rest in the crotch, both tied to the line
Whale's violent run prevents second iron from being darted
Second iron tossed overboard, becoming a dangling danger
chapters.setting: Whaleboat at the bow
contentNotes: Sailors sometimes die in fatal casualties when the second iron is thrown overboard

chapters.summary: The crew tows Stubb's dead whale toward the Pequod on a calm night. Ahab drops a lantern, gives orders, and goes into his cabin without coming back on deck until morning. The whale is moored alongside the ship, and thousands of sharks feed on it noisily. Stubb orders a steak cut from the whale and eats it at the capstan by lantern light. He makes the cook, old Fleece, preach to the sharks to quiet them. Stubb then questions Fleece about his age, birth, and faith, and gives him orders for cooking the whale. Fleece leaves muttering that the whale should eat him.

Ahab gives orders and goes into his cabin
Whale is moored alongside the ship
Stubb has a steak cut and eats it at the capstan
Stubb makes old Fleece preach to the sharks
chapters.setting: Pequod at sea, at night, beside a moored whale
contentNotes: A whale is killed and cut up
Sharks feed on a dead whale
Racial dialect and racial stereotyping of the cook, Fleece
Strong profanity and swearing
Cannibalism is mentioned in a metaphor about sea fights

chapters.summary: The narrator explains that people have long eaten whales and other sea creatures. He tells of whale tongue prized in France, porpoise dishes in England, and Greenland castaways who lived on whale scraps. He says the whale is too rich to be a fine dish, and describes eating spermaceti and whale brains. He then argues that people who eat meat are no better than cannibals. He ends by pointing out that many everyday items, like knife handles and quill pens, come from animals too.
keyEvents: Narrator explains the history of eating whales and porpoises

chapters.summary: The crew did not cut in the captured Sperm Whale that night, since that work would take all hands. Instead, after supper, Stubb set an anchor-watch. Queequeg and a forecastle seaman came on deck, lowered three lanterns over the side, and drove their whaling-spades into the crowds of sharks around the carcass. The sharks snapped at each other and even bit their own bodies. A dead shark nearly took Queequeg's hand off when he tried to shut its jaw. Queequeg complained about the god who made sharks.

chapters.summary: On a Saturday night the crew of the Pequod works on a dead whale. The men rig the large cutting tackles and lash them to the lower mast-head. Starbuck and Stubb, the mates, cut a hole for the blubber hook above the whale's fin. The windlass hoists the blubber, and the ship leans far over as the strip peels off. A harpooneer slices the mass in two so the upper strip can be lowered into the blubber-room. The crew sings, works hard, and swears as the work goes on.

chapters.summary: The narrator studies the skin of the whale and argues that the thick blubber is the true skin. He describes a thin, transparent outer layer and the marks and scratches on a whale's body. He explains that blubber keeps the whale warm in icy seas, since whales have lungs and warm blood. He ends by urging people to stay warm in spirit, like the whale.

chapters.summary: The crew cut loose the stripped whale carcass and let it drift away from the ship. Sharks and screaming birds fed on it, and the noise grew louder as the white mass floated farther off. The narrator then reflected on how the whale's ghost would scare later sailors. Ships would avoid the spot for years, following old warnings without question. The chapter ends by asking the reader whether he believes in ghosts.

chapters.summary: The crew beheads the sperm whale and hoists its huge head beside the Pequod. The men go below for dinner, leaving the deck quiet under a still copper calm. Ahab comes up alone, props himself on Stubb's spade, and speaks to the hanging head as if it were the Sphynx. He asks it to tell its secrets, since it has seen many drownings and terrible sights. A cry of 'Sail ho!' comes from the masthead, and Ahab's mood lifts. He says the cry might convert a better man and wishes the breeze would come to his calm.

chapters.summary: The Pequod signals a passing whale-ship, which turns out to be the Jeroboam. Captain Mayhew refuses to come aboard because his crew has a sickness. Stubb recognizes a crazy man named Gabriel, a former Shaker prophet who controls the crew. Mayhew tells how Gabriel warned against hunting Moby Dick, and how Mate Macey was killed by the whale when he attacked it anyway. Ahab asks for a letter for one of Mayhew's officers. Starbuck passes it down on a split pole, but Gabriel grabs it and sends it back to the Pequod. Then the Jeroboam's boat rows away.

chapters.summary: The crew works to cut in and strip a dead whale. Queequeg goes down onto the whale's back to set the blubber-hook, and Ishmael holds him by a monkey-rope. Ishmael reflects on how tied together every person is. Sharks circle, and Tashtego and Daggoo strike at them with whale-spades near Queequeg. When Queequeg climbs out, the steward offers him ginger and water. Stubb angrily objects, saying it should be grog for a harpooneer, and the steward admits Aunt Charity sent the ginger. Stubb fetches spirits from the lockers for Queequeg and throws the ginger away.

chapters.summary: The Pequod sees Right Whales nearby and sends out Stubb's and Flask's boats. The boats chase a whale that drags them close to the ship, and the crew cuts loose just in time. After a hard fight the whale dies and is towed alongside. While the men work, Stubb and Flask talk about Fedallah, whom Stubb calls the devil. Stubb jokes about ducking him and cutting off his tail. Flask says a ship with two whale heads on her sides can never capsize. The Pequod tilts toward the sperm whale's head, then steadies as the right whale's head is added. Fedallah studies the right whale's head and the lines on his hand, and the crew talks about these strange events.

He explains that a whale's eyes sit far to the sides, so it sees two separate pictures and cannot see straight ahead. He describes the whale's tiny ear, which has an opening only in the Sperm Whale. He compares the head to a shoe, a bass-viol, and a tree with a bird's nest. He describes the lower lip, the mouth, the whalebone blinds, and the tongue. He explains that the Right Whale and the Sperm Whale have very different heads. He ends by comparing the two dead whales' expressions, calling the Right Whale a Stoic and the Sperm Whale a Platonian.

chapters.summary: The narrator asks the reader to study the front of the sperm whale's head as a physiologist would. He describes it as a blind, boneless wall covered in a tough envelope that rebounds harpoons and lances. He compares it to a cushioned wad that protects ships in crowded docks. He suggests the whale's honeycomb-like inner cells might connect to the outer air, which would give its head great force. He ends by saying a reader who doubts the whale's power is only a provincial and sentimentalist in Truth.

chapters.summary: The narrator explained the inner structure of the sperm whale's head before the baling of the case. He divided the head into two parts, the bony lower part and the oily upper part. He compared the upper part, called the case, to the great Heidelburgh Tun. He described how valuable spermaceti hardens after death and how much of it is lost. He ended by saying the tapping of the tun would be a dangerous operation.

chapters.summary: Tashtego climbs to the top of the whale's head and lowers a bucket into the cistern to bale out sperm oil. While he works, he slips and falls head-first into the Tun. Daggoo, who first recovers, is hoisted up on the bucket. One hook holding the head tears out, and the head drops into the sea. Queequeg dives in with his sword, cuts a hole in the head, and pulls Tashtego out by the hair. The narrator then reflects on the accident and compares it to other strange deaths.

chapters.summary: The narrator thinks about reading the face of the Sperm Whale, which is hard because the whale has no proper nose. He says the whale's huge forehead is the most impressive view of him, and that its grandeur makes it look godlike. He also says the whale's silence and lack of a tongue suggest great genius, and that the whale might have been worshipped by ancient peoples. He ends by saying that even great scholars could not read a face fully, so he can only show the brow to the reader and invite them to read it.

chapters.summary: The narrator explains that the sperm whale's brain is very small and hidden behind its huge skull and mass of sperm. He says some whalemen think the sperm mass is the real brain. He compares the whale's skull to a human skull and claims the whale's reversed skull shows a lack of self-esteem and veneration. He then argues that a man's character shows in his spine, and he gives the whale's large spinal cord and hump a meaning tied to firmness and an unbending spirit.

chapters.summary: The Pequod meets the German ship Jungfrau, captained by Derick De Deer, who comes over asking for oil for his lamp. Derick sees a pod of whales and rushes off to chase them. The Pequod's boats join the chase, and Derick is thrown from his boat when the whale rushes away. The Pequod's men harpoon a large old whale with a bad wound and blind eyes. It dies after spouting blood. The whale is tied to the ship, but it sinks and drags the Pequod over, and Queequeg cuts the chains so the ship can right itself. The Jungfrau then chases a Fin-Back whale instead.

chapters.summary: The narrator argued that whaling is an honorable and very old calling. He said Perseus was the first whaleman, since he harpooned a sea monster to save Andromeda. He claimed St. George's dragon was really a whale, and that Hercules and Jonah should also count as whalemen. He said the Hindu god Vishnoo became a whale to rescue sacred books from the bottom of the sea. He ended by saying no club can match the whaleman's list of heroes.

He pointed to a Bible picture of a whale with two spouts and to the small swallow of the Right Whale. He also doubted that Jonah could survive inside a whale and reach Nineveh in three days. The narrator rejects these doubts as proud and foolish, noting that Turks still believe the story.

chapters.summary: Queequeg greases the bottom of his boat so it will slide faster. Later, whales are seen, but they flee the ship. Stubb's boat chases the fastest whale. Tashtego plants one harpoon, but the whale keeps swimming hard, so the crew cannot get close. Stubb uses pitchpoling, throwing a long lance from a rocking boat. The lance strikes the whale's life spot, and the whale spouts blood. Stubb jokes about drinking punch from the spout. He throws again and again until the whale dies.

chapters.summary: The narrator explains how the sperm whale breathes. Unlike fish, the whale has lungs and must rise to the surface to breathe through its spiracle on top of its head. He describes how the whale stores air in a network of blood vessels so it can stay underwater for an hour or more. The narrator then asks whether the whale's spout is water or only vapor. He says no one can settle the question, and that the spout can sting skin and may blind a person. He offers his own idea that the spout is mist, comparing it to the steam rising from deep thinkers. The chapter ends with his reflections on doubt and faith.

chapters.summary: The narrator praises the whale's tail as the most beautiful and powerful part of the sperm whale. He describes its size, its three layers of fibres, and its strong muscles. He explains five ways the whale uses its tail: swimming, striking boats, sweeping, lobtailing, and peaking its flukes. He compares the tail to an elephant's trunk and says the whale's tail is far stronger. He ends by saying he cannot fully understand the whale, since it seems to have no face.

chapters.summary: The Pequod sails toward the Straits of Sunda, where Ahab plans to pass into the Javan sea. Malay pirates chase the ship from behind, but the Pequod outruns them. The crew spots a large herd of Sperm Whales and gives chase. The whales panic and gather into a tight herd. Queequeg harpoons one whale, which drags the boat into the middle of the herd. There the crew finds a calm lake with mother whales and calves. A wounded whale tangled in the lines then stirs up the herd, forcing the boat to escape. Queequeg loses his hat. Only one whale is captured in the end.

The author called the older male the schoolmaster and said old whales usually live alone. He also said that when a female is hurt, her group stays close to her, but young males leave a wounded comrade.

chapters.summary: The narrator explains the whaling laws about fast-fish and loose-fish. A fast-fish belongs to the party fastened to it, and a loose-fish belongs to whoever catches it first. He describes a famous English lawsuit, where a crew took a whale another crew had lost, and Lord Ellenborough ruled for the defendants. The narrator then compares these two rules to ownership and power in wider society, such as landlords, bankers, and nations. He ends by asking the reader whether he is a loose-fish and a fast-fish too.

He tells of Dover-area mariners who killed a whale, only to have a learned gentleman seize it for the Lord Warden, the Duke of Wellington. The men protest, but the Duke keeps the money. The narrator then asks why the King and Queen divide the whale this way, quoting Plowdon and William Prynne, and jokes about whalebone and sturgeon.

chapters.summary: Pip, a young Black crew member, is made a temporary boat oarsman after another man's hand is injured. On his second whale hunt, he jumps from the boat after a whale's rap startles him, and the line tangles around his chest. Tashtego asks whether to cut the line, and Stubb orders it cut, so the whale is lost and Pip is saved. Stubb warns Pip not to jump again. A sailor called the mincer hauls it to the forecastle, strips off its dark pelt, and turns the pelt inside out to dry in the rigging. He then slips into the skin like a clergyman's robe. chapters.summary: On the Pequod, Stubb ordered the try-works started around nine at night so the crew could render whale blubber into oil. By midnight the fires burned fiercely, and the harpooneers fed the pots while the watch rested nearby. The narrator stood at the helm, dozed, and turned around until he realized his mistake and turned back to the compass just in time. He then reflected on the danger of staring too long into fire and on the difference between wisdom and madness.

chapters.summary: The narrator asks the reader to picture the Pequod's forecastle, where off-duty sailors sleep under many lamps. He compares them to figures in a shrine. He then explains that whalemen burn lamps freely, refilling old bottles with pure whale oil from the try-works. He says this oil is fresher than the oil ordinary sailors on merchant ships can get, and that whalemen go out to hunt for it themselves.

chapters.summary: The narrator explained how hot whale oil was poured into casks and rolled down into the hold. The crew then scrubbed the ship until its decks shone white, and the sailors cleaned themselves and dressed up. Soon a cry of 'There she blows!' sent the men off to hunt another whale. The narrator compared this endless cycle to human life, where people must start over again and again. He ended by remembering Pythagoras, a wise man he once taught to splice a rope.

chapters.summary: Ahab often paused at the binnacle and the mainmast during his walks on the quarter-deck. One morning he stopped before the gold doubloon nailed to the mast and studied its figures. He said the coin mirrored each man's own self, and that man is born in pain and dies in pangs. Starbuck read the coin as a sad sign of God's dark valley and bright sun. Stubb read the zodiac as the story of a man's life, full of jokes. Flask counted the cigars the coin could buy. The old Manxman predicted the White Whale would be raised in a month and a day. Pip repeated grammar lessons and seemed mad. Queequeg and Fedallah also looked at the coin.

chapters.summary: The Pequod meets the English ship Samuel Enderby, whose captain has also lost an arm to the White Whale. Ahab struggles to climb aboard because he has only one leg, but the crew lifts him with a blubber-hook. The English captain tells how the whale tangled his line, smashed his boat, and wounded him. Ship's surgeon Bunger adds his own story and jokes about the captain's drinking. Ahab grows fierce and eager to know where the whale was last seen. When Bunger reaches for his arm with a lancet, Ahab shoves him away and orders his boat readied. He returns to the Pequod without taking any more information from the English captain.

chapters.summary: The narrator describes the English ship Samuel Enderby, named after the merchant Samuel Enderby, and the whaling house of Enderby & Sons. He recalls the history of English and Nantucket whaling, including the Amelia's voyage in 1778 and the Syren's cruise to Japan in 1819. He tells of visiting the Samuel Enderby at midnight off Patagonia, where the crew drank flip and ate beef and dumplings. He then describes an old Dutch book on whaling, Dan Coopman, which lists huge stores of food and drink for Dutch whalers. He calculates that each Dutch sailor had about two barrels of beer for a twelve-week cruise. He concludes that English whalers also enjoyed good food and drink, and the chapter ends with the decanter emptied.

chapters.summary: Ishmael explains that he will describe the whale's bones, since he once cut open a small young whale and later studied a huge skeleton. He recalls his visit to the palm villa of his friend King Tranquo in Tranque. There, a dead sperm whale's skeleton had been placed in a temple, where priests kept a flame burning in its skull. Ishmael walked through the ribs with a ball of twine and measured the skeleton with a green rod until the priests quarreled and shouted at him. He then notes other whale skeletons in England and America that people can check his figures against. Last, he says his measurements are tattooed on his right arm.

chapters.summary: The narrator gives a plain estimate of the living Sperm Whale's size and weight, saying a whale of about ninety feet could weigh at least ninety tons. He then describes the skeleton at Tranque, which measures seventy-two feet and is much smaller than the living whale. He describes the ten pairs of ribs, noting that the largest rib is only about half the true depth of the living body. He says the whale can only be truly understood at sea, not by studying bones. Last, he describes the forty-odd vertebrae, which tapered to small bones that had been stolen by the priest's children to play marbles.

chapters.summary: The narrator describes the whale as a subject too large for ordinary words. He claims to be a stone-mason and ditch-digger, and he explains that whale fossils from the Tertiary period link ancient and modern creatures. He tells of skulls found in Paris and Antwerp, and of a skeleton found in Alabama in 1842, which Owen renamed Zeuglodon. He then points to whale carvings on an Egyptian ceiling and to John Leo's account of a temple with whale-bone rafters. He ends by urging Nantucket whalemen to worship there.

contentNotes: Refers to enslaved people in Alabama as 'credulous slaves' in a condescending, dated way
