chapters.summary: The narrator asks whether whales have shrunk over time. He compares modern whales with fossil whales, and with ancient and older writers' tall claims about giant whales, which he doubts. He argues that whalers cannot wipe out whales as hunters wiped out the buffalo, because whale hunting is slow and whales can hide in the far seas and polar ice. He notes that whales live long and that several generations live at once. In the end he calls the whale immortal as a species, though each whale dies.

chapters.setting: Not a specific place; general discussion of whales and the sea
contentNotes: Describes the mass slaughter of buffalo and the killing of whales, with no graphic detail

chapters.summary: Ahab's ivory leg was shaken when he jumped onto a thwart of his boat and then turned sharply on his own deck. He did not trust it. Ahab had earlier been found unconscious on the ground at Nantucket, because his leg had been knocked out of place and nearly pierced his groin. He thought about how grief breeds more grief. He then called the carpenter and ordered a new leg made from the best jaw-ivory that night. He also had the forge brought up from the hold so the blacksmith could make iron fittings.

chapters.summary: The narrator described the Pequod's carpenter, a man skilled in many trades on a long whaling voyage. He worked at a heavy vice-bench near the try-works. He filed a belaying pin, built a cage for a captured bird, and treated a sprained wrist. He also drilled a sailor's ears and tried to pull a sailor's tooth. The narrator said the carpenter seemed stolid and heartless, working almost without thought, like a handy tool. Yet some hidden life in him kept him muttering to himself.

He talks of Prometheus, the blacksmith, and of how a lost leg still feels present to a man. He tells the carpenter that a living thing might stand where he stands, and he says the carpenter might feel hell's pains without a body. Ahab then leaves, and the carpenter says the crew, Stubb, and Starbuck all think Ahab is queer. The carpenter promises to finish the leg within the hour.

chapters.summary: The crew pumps the Pequod and finds a good deal of oil coming up with the water, so the casks below must be leaking. Starbuck goes to the cabin to report it. Ahab is studying charts near Formosa and the Bashee Isles and refuses to stop for repairs. Starbuck argues, and Ahab seizes a loaded musket and aims it at him, ordering him on deck. Starbuck leaves with a warning that Ahab should beware of himself. Ahab then orders the sails shortened and the Burtons hoisted to fix the leak.

chapters.summary: The crew searched for a leak deep in the ship's hold while Queequeg fell ill with a fever that nearly killed him. Believing he was dying, he asked for a coffin like the canoes of Nantucket. The carpenter built it from old dark wood, and Queequeg lay in it with his harpoon, biscuits, and his small god Yojo. Pip called out about a coward who jumped from a whale-boat. Then Queequeg suddenly rallied, saying he had a duty ashore left undone.

chapters.summary: The Pacific sea opens wide before the Pequod. The narrator praises its calm blue waters and says it seems to hold a hidden soul. He describes it as the center of the world, with its waves washing many lands. Ahab stands at his usual place by the mizen rigging. He smells the sweet air of the Bashee isles and the salt sea, knowing the White Whale swims somewhere ahead. His purpose grows stronger, and in his sleep he cries out that the White Whale spouts thick blood.

chapters.summary: Perth, an old blacksmith, kept his portable forge on deck and worked constantly for the crew, mending harpoons, lances, and boat gear. He rarely complained. The mariners eventually learned his sad story. On a bitter winter night, he was caught out on a road and lost the feet to the cold. Earlier, his happy home had been ruined by the Bottle Conjuror, which the text uses as a figure for drink. His wife and children died, the house was sold, and he became a homeless wanderer. The chapter ends with him deciding to go whaling.

chapters.summary: The Pequod sails deep into the Japanese cruising ground, and its crew spends many hours in the whale boats chasing whales with little success. On calm days the sea seems gentle and beautiful, and the narrator reflects on how peaceful moods pass quickly, like the storms and calms that fill life. Ahab feels a brief softening in these quiet scenes. Starbuck gazes down into the golden water and says he chooses to believe rather than remember the dangers of the sea. Stubb then declares that he has always been jolly.

chapters.summary: The Pequod meets the Bachelor, a Nantucket ship returning home after a very successful whaling trip. The Bachelor is full of sperm oil and its crew celebrates loudly with drums, dancing, and music. Captain Ahab stands gloomy on the Pequod while the other captain calls out to him to come aboard. Ahab asks whether the other captain has seen the White Whale, and the captain says he does not believe in it. Ahab refuses the invitation, calls the Bachelor's captain a fool, and orders his ship to sail on. The two ships part, and Ahab looks at a small vial of Nantucket sand.

chapters.summary: After the Pequod met the Bachelor, its crew saw more whales and killed four of them. Ahab killed one of these whales. As the sun set, the whale died slowly, turning its head toward the sun. Ahab sat in his boat and watched it. He thought about the sun, the dark sea, and the faith of living things. He then spoke to the sea and called its waves his foster-brothers.

chapters.summary: Four whales were killed the evening before. The windward one was too far away to tow, so Ahab's boat stayed beside it all night. Ahab woke and spoke with the Parsee, who was watching sharks around the dead whale. Ahab said he had dreamed of hearses again. The Parsee repeated his prophecies that Ahab cannot die until two hearses are seen at sea and that only hemp can kill him. Ahab laughed and called himself immortal on land and sea. At dawn the crew woke, and by noon the dead whale was brought to the ship.

chapters.summary: The crew waited for the order to sail for the equator. At high noon, Ahab took a sun sighting with his quadrant to find his latitude. He cursed the instrument and wished he could see farther than the sun. Then he smashed the quadrant on the deck and stamped it to pieces, saying he would navigate by the compass and log line instead. The Parsee watched silently and then walked away. Ahab ordered the ship turned. Starbuck reflected on how a fire burns down to ashes, and Stubb answered that Ahab must play the hand he was dealt.

chapters.summary: A fierce typhoon struck the Pequod in the Japanese seas and tore away her sails. A wave stove in Ahab's whale-boat. Starbuck urged the crew to turn toward home, while Stubb tried to keep his spirits up with a song. Pale flames called corpusants burned at the tops of the three masts and on Ahab's harpoon. Ahab held the burning harpoon, made the crew swear to hunt the White Whale, and blew out the flame. Many sailors ran from him in fear.

Ahab told him to lash everything and strike nothing. When Starbuck asked about the anchors, Ahab again ordered nothing moved. Ahab mocked Starbuck, called the top of the mast his brain-truck, and joked about taking medicine for colic.

Stubb teases Flask about his earlier worry that Ahab's ship was a danger, like a ship loaded with powder and matches. He argues that lightning rods make a ship safe and that sensible men stay calm. As they work, Stubb jokes about wet clothes and the anchors, and his own hat blows away. He ends by calling it a nasty night.

Starbuck goes below to report to Captain Ahab and finds the loaded muskets in the cabin. He thinks about killing Ahab while he sleeps, and he holds a musket to the old man's door. Ahab mutters in his sleep about Moby Dick. Starbuck puts the musket back in its rack and leaves. He tells Stubb to wake Ahab and report the change.

chapters.summary: The next morning the Pequod sails on a rough sea with a strong wind. Ahab feels proud and speaks to the ship as if it were the sun's chariot. The steersman says the ship is heading east, and Ahab angrily strikes him. Ahab sees that the compasses point east while the ship is really going west. He blames the thunder from the night before. Starbuck says he has never seen this happen to him. Ahab uses a lance, a top-maul, and a sail-maker's needle to make a new magnetic needle. He hangs it over the compass and shows the crew it points true. The men look and then walk away, and Ahab looks proud and fierce.

Ahab rushes to the stern, takes Pip's hand, and leads him to his cabin. He declares that Pip will live with him from then on.

At sunrise a sailor falls from the mast-head into the sea and drowns. The life-buoy is dropped but sinks, since its cask fills with water. No light cask can be found to replace it, so Queequeg suggests using his coffin. Starbuck orders the carpenter to make it into a life-buoy. Ahab teased the Carpenter about being a leg-maker, an undertaker, and a jack-of-all-trades. He asked whether the Carpenter ever sang while he worked. Ahab then thought about how the dreaded coffin had become a sign of help and hope. He told the Carpenter to stop the tapping and went below with Pip.

Gardiner's young son is in the missing boat, and he begs Ahab for help. Ahab refuses, saying he must go on, and the Rachel sails away still searching.

Pip begs to go with him, but Ahab refuses and says his ivory foot will still be heard above. After Ahab leaves, Pip is alone in the cabin. He imagines a gathering of captains and officers and talks to them about a missing Pip. He decides he will stay below, even as the ship seems to strike rocks.

chapters.summary: Ahab believes he is close to Moby Dick and grows more fixed in his purpose. His crew goes quiet and afraid, and Fedallah seems almost like a shadow. Ahab stays on deck day and night and rarely speaks to Fedallah. When no spout is seen for several days, Ahab climbs to the masthead in a basket. He puts Starbuck in charge of the rope that holds him up. A savage hawk circles him and then snatches his hat and flies off with it. The hat falls into the sea, and it is never returned to him.

chapters.summary: The Pequod sails on and sights another ship, the Delight. Its broken boat hangs from the shears, and the Delight's captain says the White Whale has not been killed. Ahab holds up a harpoon and swears to strike the whale. The captain says five of his strong men died, and he buries one of them at sea. The body splashes into the water as the Pequod turns away. A voice from the Delight warns that the Pequod cannot escape the coffin-like life-buoy at its stern.

chapters.summary: On a calm, clear day, Ahab leans over the side of the ship and remembers his forty years at sea. He tells Starbuck he feels old and regrets the lonely life he has led, and he thinks of his wife and child in Nantucket. Starbuck begs him to sail home and give up the chase of Moby Dick. Ahab wonders whether fate controls him, then sees Fedallah leaning over the same rail. Starbuck, pale with despair, walks away.

chapters.summary: That night Ahab smelled a whale and had the ship's course changed. At dawn the crew saw Moby Dick ahead. Ahab climbed to the masthead and shouted that it was the White Whale, then lowered the boats. The whale stayed calm at first, then rose under Ahab's boat and bit it in two. Ahab was thrown into the sea and was pulled out by Stubb's crew. The Pequod came up and drove the whale away. The crew tried to chase him with the ship. As the day ended, Ahab looked at the broken boat and spoke harshly to Stubb and Starbuck. He stayed by the scuttle until dawn.

chapters.summary: At daybreak Ahab orders the crew to keep chasing Moby Dick. The White Whale breaches far off, and the boats race toward him. Moby Dick charges the three boats and tangles their lines. Ahab cuts loose the tangled harpoons, but Stubb and Flask's boats are smashed and their crews thrown into the sea. Moby Dick then strikes Ahab's boat and flips it over. The crews are rescued, but the Parsee is missing and Ahab's ivory leg is snapped off. Starbuck begs Ahab to stop the chase, but Ahab refuses. Through the night the crew repairs the boats, and the carpenter makes Ahab a new leg.

chapters.summary: On the third day of the chase, Ahab sees the white whale again and is lowered into a boat with his crew. Sharks follow the boat and bite at the oars. The whale tangles and drags the body of the Parsee, and then he rams the Pequod. The whale smashes the ship's bow and sinks it. Ahab is caught in the line and pulled from the boat into the sea. The Pequod and its crew go down, and the sea closes over them. Only a few small birds fly over the place where the ship sank.

chapters.summary: The narrator, the only survivor of the wreck, was drawn into the whirlpool left by the sinking ship. He circled the dark center until a coffin life-buoy shot up from the sea and floated beside him. For almost a day and night he drifted on the calm water, passing sharks and sea-hawks that did not harm him. On the second day the ship Rachel picked him up. She had been searching for her missing children and found only one more orphan.

synopsis: Ishmael, a young sailor, goes to New Bedford and meets Queequeg, a tattooed harpooner from a faraway island. The two become close friends and sign on to the whaling ship Pequod, captained by Ahab. Ahab lost a leg to a huge white whale called Moby Dick and is obsessed with revenge. He hides his purpose at first, then openly swears his crew to the hunt. The Pequod hunts many whales, and the narrator describes whaling in great detail, from cutting up blubber to making oil. Ahab grows more driven, ignoring warnings from Starbuck, his mate, and from strange omens. Ahab's search finally finds Moby Dick. In three days of fighting, the whale destroys the boats, takes Ahab down with a line, and sinks the Pequod. Ishmael alone survives, floating on a coffin life-buoy until a ship rescues him.
